stages.title: Birds, aircraft and the idea of flight
stages.hook: A bird flaps and goes up. A plane does not flap at all, yet it flies. How can that be?
explain: Flying means staying up in the air and moving through it. Birds, bats and insects fly. People build machines to fly too.
A bird has wings. It pushes air with them. A plane has wings too, but its wings stay still. Engines push the plane forward, and air flows over the wings.
Air is a real thing, even if we cannot see it. Wings use moving air to hold a bird or a plane up. That is the big idea of flight.

example.q: A pigeon and a small plane both fly. What do both of them have?
steps: Look at the pigeon. It has wings.
Look at the plane. It has wings too.
Both move through the air.

analogies.nature: A seed with a little wing spins down from a tree. The wing catches the air and slows the fall.
analogies.sea: A gull glides over the waves without flapping. It rides the moving air.
analogies.home: Hold your hand flat out of a car window, with a grown-up in the car. You can feel the air push your hand.
analogies.sport: A kite is like a wing. Run with it and it lifts into the sky.

stages.mnemonic: Wings plus moving air means flying up there!
terms: Moving through the air without touching the ground.
The flat part that helps a bird or plane fly.
The invisible gas all around us.

misc.wrong: Air is nothing, so it cannot hold things up.
misc.right: Air is made of tiny bits of gas. When air moves over wings, it can push them up.

stages.limits: This is a simple picture. Real birds and planes use many careful tricks to fly.

trip.prompt: Look at the pictures of wings. Which bird has the biggest wings?

questions.why: A sparrow has wings and can fly. The others cannot.

questions.q: What do birds and planes both have?
questions.why: Both have wings. Only birds have feathers.

questions.q: What moves over a wing when a plane flies?
questions.why: Air flows over the wings and helps hold the plane up.

questions.q: Can we see air?
o: No, but we can feel it move
Yes, it is blue like water in the sky
No, because it is not really there

questions.q: A plane does not flap its wings. What makes it go forward?
questions.why: Engines push the plane forward through the air.

questions.q: A kite flies when you run with it. Why?
o: Moving air flows past the kite
The kite is very heavy and falls

Moving air flows past it and pushes it down

questions.why: A bee is tiny, a sparrow is small, an eagle is bigger, and a passenger plane is the biggest.

questions.q: Match each flyer to what it is.
questions.why: An eagle is a bird, a helicopter is a machine, and a bat is a flying mammal.

questions.q: A seed with a wing falls slowly from a tree. What does the wing do?
questions.why: The wing catches the air and slows the fall.

questions.q: A paper plane has no engine. What gives it its first push?
questions.why: Your throw gives the push. Then the wings use the air to glide.

panel.q: Why can a bird glide without flapping for a while?
o: Air moving past its still wings holds it up
Its light feathers make it weightless in the sky
The warm sun pulls it up with heat rays all the time
A bird must flap its wings or it drops at once
panel.why: Moving air over the wings can hold the bird up for a time, but it slowly sinks.

panel.q: Why does a plane need to move to fly?
o: Moving makes air flow over the wings
Moving keeps the engine nice and cool
Moving makes the plane much lighter
Planes can fly while sitting still
panel.why: Air must flow over the wings to make the lift that holds the plane up.

panel.q: A ball is thrown and does not fly for long. A bird flies for hours. What is the main difference?
o: The bird has wings and keeps pushing
The ball is too round to fly for very long
The bird is much lighter than the air around it
The ball has no bright colour on it, so it falls
panel.why: The bird has wings and muscles that keep making lift and thrust. The ball has only the first throw.

teach.model: A bird has wings. When the bird moves, air flows over its wings. The moving air helps hold the bird up. The bird flaps to push itself forward.

points.ask: What part of the bird helps it fly?
What does the wing use to stay up?
Does the bird need to move?

stages.title: Parts of an aeroplane
stages.hook: Look at a picture of a plane. Can you find the part that sticks out on each side? What is it for?
explain: An aeroplane has a body called the fuselage. People and bags sit inside it. The nose is at the front.
The wings stick out from the sides. They hold the plane up. The tail is at the back. It keeps the plane straight and steady.
The engines push the plane forward. The wheels are called landing gear. They help the plane roll on the runway.

example.q: Which part holds the plane up?
steps: Think about what sticks out on each side.
The wings are there.
Moving air over the wings lifts the plane.

analogies.home: The fuselage is like the body of a toy. The wings are like arms that stick out.
analogies.sea: The tail of a plane is like the rudder of a boat. It helps keep the way straight.
analogies.sport: The landing gear is like roller skates. It lets the plane roll.
analogies.nature: A bird has a body, two wings and a tail. A plane has the same three parts.

stages.mnemonic: Nose, body, wings, tail, wheels, and engines to sail!
terms: The long body of the plane.
Holds the plane up in the air.

misc.wrong: The engine is what holds the plane up.
misc.right: The wings hold the plane up. The engine pushes the plane forward.

stages.limits: Not all planes look the same. Some have propellers and some have jet engines.

trip.prompt: Find the wings, tail and engines in a picture of a plane.

questions.q: What is the body of a plane called?
questions.why: The fuselage is the long body of the plane.

questions.q: Which part helps the plane roll on the ground?
questions.why: The landing gear has wheels.

questions.q: Which part is at the back of the plane?
questions.why: The tail is at the back.

questions.q: What do engines do?
questions.why: Engines make the push that moves the plane forward.

questions.q: What do wings do?
questions.why: Wings help hold the plane up when air flows over them.

questions.q: A toy plane has no tail. What might go wrong?
o: It may wobble and not fly straight
It will be too quiet to hear

It will fly faster for ever and ever

questions.q: Match each plane part to its job.
questions.why: Each part has its own job.

questions.why: The nose is at the front. The wings are near the middle. The fuselage is the long body. The tail is at the back.

questions.q: Why are the wheels folded up inside the plane in the air?
o: So less air pushes against the plane
So the wheels can stay dry and clean
So the wheels can have a rest
So the wheels do not get lost
questions.why: Folding the wheels in makes the plane smoother, so the air pushes against it less.

questions.q: A plane lands on a long, flat road called a runway. Which part touches it first?
questions.why: The landing gear is made to touch the runway.

panel.q: Why do some planes have two wings and a tail, but no wheels on their top?
o: Wings and tail work in the air and wheels work on the ground
Wheels would make the plane fly up much higher
The top is only there for passengers to sit on
Wings are used for rolling along the ground and tail for lifting
panel.why: Each part has a job in a certain place. Wheels are underneath so they can touch the ground.

panel.q: A plane with big wings can carry a heavy load. Why?
o: Bigger wings can make more lift
Big wings are heavier, so they hold more
Big wings make more noise and shake the load
Wings do not matter for a heavy load
panel.why: A bigger wing area can make more lift.

panel.q: Which two parts must work together for a plane to go up the runway and into the sky?
panel.why: Engines give forward speed. Then air over the wings lifts the plane.

teach.topic: The main parts of an aeroplane
teach.model: A plane has a long body called the fuselage. The wings stick out and hold it up. The tail keeps it steady. The engines push it forward, and the wheels help it land.

points.ask: Which part holds the plane up?
What pushes the plane forward?
What keeps the plane steady?
How does the plane touch the ground?

stages.title: Parts of a helicopter
stages.hook: A helicopter has no big wings. How does it go straight up and stay still in the air?
explain: A helicopter has long blades on top. They are called the rotor. The rotor spins very fast.
The spinning blades act like wings. Air flows over them and they pull the helicopter up. That is why it can go straight up and down.
A helicopter has a long tail with a small rotor on it. This tail rotor stops the body from spinning round. The body is called the fuselage, and the pilot sits at the front.

example.q: A helicopter hovers. What is spinning above it?
steps: Look at the top of the helicopter.
There are long blades.
These blades are the main rotor.

analogies.home: A ceiling fan spins blades to move air. A helicopter rotor moves air too, but down.
analogies.nature: A maple seed spins like a tiny helicopter as it falls.
analogies.sport: A spinning top stays up while it spins. A rotor needs to spin to work.
analogies.city: A rescue helicopter can hover over a roof and lower help to people.

stages.mnemonic: Spin, spin, spin on top, the helicopter will not drop!
terms: A small spinning fan on the tail.
Stay in one place in the air.
One long arm of the rotor.

misc.wrong: A helicopter has wings like a plane.
misc.right: A helicopter's spinning blades work like wings. They are called rotor blades.

stages.limits: This is a simple picture. Real helicopters have many other parts.

trip.prompt: Find the main rotor and the tail rotor in a picture.

questions.q: What are the spinning blades on top of a helicopter called?
questions.why: They are called the rotor.

questions.q: What does a helicopter do when it hovers?
o: Stays in one place in the air
Drives along a road like a bus
Lands on a soft cloud to sleep
questions.why: To hover is to stay in one spot in the air.

questions.q: Can a helicopter go straight up?
questions.why: Spinning rotor blades can pull it straight up.

questions.q: Where is the small rotor on a helicopter?
questions.why: The tail rotor is on the long tail.

questions.q: What do the spinning blades act like?
questions.why: Rotor blades are like wings that move round.

questions.q: A helicopter needs a long runway to take off. True or false?
o: False. It can lift off straight up
True. It always needs a long runway
True. It has no engine at all
False. It cannot take off anywhere

questions.q: Match each helicopter part to what it does.
questions.why: Each part has a job. Skids are like feet for landing.

questions.q: Put these in order for a helicopter trip.
questions.why: The rotor must spin first. Then it lifts, hovers and lands.

questions.q: A helicopter's rotor stops spinning in the air. What happens?

questions.q: Why would a helicopter help rescue people on a mountain?
o: It can hover and land in small spaces
It is the fastest thing in the sky
It carries its own long runway
It never needs any fuel at all

panel.q: Why does the main rotor spin and not stay still?

Blades only look nice when they spin

panel.q: If there were no tail rotor, what might the body do?

panel.q: How is a helicopter different from a plane?
o: Its wings spin and it can hover

It flies only on top of the water

points.ask: What is on top of a helicopter?
What do the blades do?
What does that do for the helicopter?

stages.title: Air and atmospheric motion
stages.hook: You cannot see wind. How do you know it is there?
explain: Air is all around us. Moving air is called wind. We feel it on our skin and see it move leaves and flags.
The air around Earth is called the atmosphere. Low down, the air is thick. High up, the air is thin, with less air to breathe.
The sun warms the ground. Warm air rises and cooler air moves in to take its place. That moving air is wind. Birds and planes fly in this moving air.

example.q: A flag waves on a pole. What does that tell you?
steps: The flag is moving.
Something is pushing it.
Moving air, or wind, is pushing it.

analogies.home: Blow on a feather. The air from your mouth moves it.
analogies.sea: Sailors use the wind to push their boats along.
analogies.farm: A windmill turns when the wind blows.
analogies.sport: A kite flies high on a windy day.

stages.mnemonic: Warm air goes up, cool air comes in. That moving air is wind!
terms: The layer of air around Earth.
Air with less stuff in it, high up.

misc.wrong: There is no air in the sky when it is calm.
misc.right: Air is always there, even when it is still. Wind is just air that moves.

stages.limits: This is a simple idea. Wind has many causes, and weather is complicated.

trip.prompt: Look at the picture of the layers of air. Where do planes fly?

questions.q: What do we call air that moves?
questions.why: Moving air is called wind.

questions.q: What is the layer of air around Earth called?
questions.why: It is called the atmosphere.

questions.q: What warms the ground and the air?
questions.why: The sun warms Earth.

questions.q: Is the air high on a mountain thick or thin?
questions.why: Higher up there is less air, so it is thin.

questions.q: Warm air does what?
questions.why: Warm air is lighter than cool air around it, so it rises.

questions.q: A bird circles upward on warm rising air without flapping. Why can it do this?
o: It is lighter than a feather
questions.why: Rising warm air can carry a gliding bird upward.

questions.q: Put these winds from the gentlest to the strongest.
questions.why: The wind gets stronger as the air moves faster.

questions.q: Match the sign to what it shows.
questions.why: Moving air makes flags wave and windmills turn.

questions.q: A pilot wants to fly over very high mountains. What should the pilot know?
o: The air is thinner up there
The air is heavier up there
questions.why: Thin air at height changes how an aircraft flies.

questions.q: Why do kite-fliers like a windy day?
questions.why: The kite uses moving air to stay up.

panel.q: Why is the air thinner high up?
o: There is less air above pressing down, so it spreads out
The sun burns the air away high up there
Mountains eat the air as it rises
Clouds are heavy and push the air down low
panel.why: There is less air above pushing down on the air, so it is less crowded.

panel.q: Why does wind blow from cool places to warm places near the sea in the day?
o: Warm air rises and cooler air moves in
The sea pulls the air towards it with a rope
The moon pushes it from above
Wind blows for no reason at all

panel.q: Why does a plane flying into the wind feel the wind helping it lift?
o: More air flows over its wings

teach.model: Air is all around us. The sun warms the air. Warm air goes up and cooler air moves in. That moving air is wind.

points.ask: What is wind made of?

What does wind do?

stages.title: Lift and gravity
stages.hook: Drop a ball and it falls. A plane stays up. What stops the plane from falling?
explain: Gravity pulls everything down toward the ground. It pulls on you, on a ball and on a plane. The pull on something is called its weight.
Lift is a push up. A wing makes lift when air flows over it. If lift is as big as weight, the plane stays up.
Air moving over a wing curves and goes down behind it. The wing pushes the air down, so the air pushes the wing up. Air under the wing pushes up more than air on top pushes down.

example.q: A plane flies level. Lift is the same as weight. Does it go up, down or stay level?
steps: Lift pushes up.
Weight pulls down.
They are equal, so they cancel.

analogies.nature: A bird spreads its wings to ride the air and keep from falling.
analogies.sea: A boat floats because water pushes up. A wing is held up by air in a different way.
analogies.sport: A frisbee flies because air lifts it as it spins.
analogies.home: Hold a sheet of paper and blow over the top. The paper rises.

stages.mnemonic: Gravity pulls down. Lift pushes up. When they match, the plane stays up!
terms: A pull that draws things down to Earth.
How hard gravity pulls on something.
An upward push on a wing.
Flying straight, not up or down.

misc.wrong: Air going over the top and bottom of a wing must meet at the same time.
misc.right: This is a myth. Air over the top is not forced to arrive at the same time as air underneath. A wing makes lift by turning air downward and by having less pressure on top.

stages.limits: Lift is a bit tricky. Real scientists use careful maths to explain it.

trip.prompt: Look at the picture of air flowing around a wing. Which way does the air bend?

questions.q: Which way does gravity pull?
questions.why: Gravity pulls things down toward Earth.

questions.q: Which way does lift push a plane?
questions.why: Lift is an upward push.

questions.q: What makes lift?
questions.why: Moving air over the wings makes lift.

questions.q: A plane flies level and steady. What can you say about lift and weight?
questions.why: When they are equal, the plane does not go up or down.

questions.q: If lift gets smaller than weight, what happens?

questions.why: Weight wins and the plane goes down.

questions.q: If you hold paper and blow over the top, what does the paper do?
questions.why: Moving air over the top lowers pressure there and the paper lifts.

questions.q: Put these in order for a plane taking off.
items: Plane speeds up on the runway

questions.why: Speed gives airflow, airflow gives lift, and lift beats weight.

questions.q: Match each force to its direction.
questions.why: Lift pushes up. Weight and gravity pull down toward Earth.

questions.q: A big plane is much heavier than a small one. What must its wings make?
questions.why: More weight needs more lift to stay up.

questions.q: Which is true about air moving over a wing?
o: The wing turns the air downward
questions.why: The wing bends the air down, and the air pushes the wing up.

panel.q: Someone says air above and below a wing must reach the back at the same time. What is wrong with that?
o: It is a myth. Air above the wing actually arrives earlier
It is right. The two paths must meet at the back together
Air never moves over the wings at all
Air under the wing never reaches the back
panel.why: The equal transit time idea is a myth. Air over the top usually gets to the back first.

panel.q: Why does a plane need to keep moving to stay up?
o: Moving makes the air flow that makes lift
Stopping makes the wings much heavier
Moving keeps the engine from getting hot
It does not need to move at all, ever
panel.why: Lift needs air flowing past the wings.

panel.q: A feather falls slowly, but a stone falls fast. Why?
o: Air pushes up on the feather more compared with its weight
Gravity is gone for light things like feathers
Stones are pulled down by the moon more
Feathers are made of air inside, like balloons
panel.why: Air pushes against the feather a lot compared with its tiny weight.

teach.topic: Why a plane does not fall
teach.model: Gravity pulls the plane down. The wings make lift, which pushes the plane up. When the air flows fast over the wings, lift can be as big as the pull down. Then the plane stays in the air.

points.ask: What pulls the plane down?
What pushes the plane up?
Where does lift come from?

stages.title: Thrust and drag
stages.hook: Push your hand through water in the bath. Now push it through air. Which is harder? Why?
explain: Thrust is a push that moves a plane forward. Engines make thrust. A propeller or a jet pushes air backward, and the plane moves forward.
Drag is air pushing against the plane. It tries to slow the plane down. Drag is a pull backward.
If thrust is bigger than drag, the plane speeds up. If they are equal, the plane keeps the same speed. A smooth, thin shape has less drag.

example.q: A plane has more thrust than drag. What happens to its speed?
steps: Thrust pushes forward.
Drag pulls back.
Thrust is bigger, so the plane speeds up.

analogies.sport: A cyclist crouches low to cut through the air. That makes less drag.
analogies.sea: A thin boat slips through water more easily than a wide one.
analogies.home: Hold a big flat book out of a car window. It pushes back more than a small one. Do this only with a grown-up and safely inside the car.
analogies.nature: A fish has a smooth shape so water flows past it easily.

stages.mnemonic: Thrust goes forward, drag holds back. Smooth shapes slip on the track!
terms: A forward push on a plane.
Air pushing back against a moving thing.
Spinning blades that push air back.
A smooth shape that slips through air.

misc.wrong: Drag only happens to big things.
misc.right: Everything that moves through air feels drag, even a ball or a bird.

stages.limits: This is a simple idea. Real engines and drag are more complicated.

trip.prompt: Find a picture of a smooth shape and a flat shape in moving air. Which one has less drag?

questions.q: Which push moves a plane forward?
questions.why: Thrust pushes the plane forward.

questions.q: Which force slows a plane down?
questions.why: Drag pulls backward against the plane.

questions.q: What do engines make?
questions.why: Engines make thrust.

questions.q: Which shape has less drag?
questions.why: Smooth shapes let air slip past.

questions.q: Thrust is the same as drag. What does the plane do?
questions.why: Equal forces cancel, so the speed does not change.

questions.q: A cyclist crouches low on a fast road. Why?
questions.why: A low shape lets the air slip past more easily.

questions.q: Put these in order from the most drag to the least drag.
questions.why: Open shapes catch the most air. A pointed dart has the least.

questions.q: Match each force to what it does to a plane.
questions.why: These are the four forces of flight.

questions.q: A plane flies steady at one speed. Thrust is 5 units. What is drag?
questions.why: Steady speed means thrust and drag are equal.

questions.q: A parachute has lots of drag. Why is that useful?
questions.why: Big drag slows a falling person.

panel.q: Why do fast cars and trains have smooth, pointed noses?
panel.why: A smooth nose lets air flow around the vehicle with less pushing back.

panel.q: Why does a plane need more thrust to go faster?
o: Drag gets bigger as speed goes up
Thrust gets smaller as the speed goes up
Lift turns off when you go faster
Wings get heavier at high speed
panel.why: Faster flight means more drag, so more thrust is needed.

panel.q: A plane turns off its engine in the air. What happens to its speed?
o: It slows down because drag is still there
It stays the same for ever and ever
It speeds up quickly, as the air pushes
It stops at once in mid-air and drops
panel.why: Without thrust, drag slows the plane.

teach.model: Thrust is the push that moves a plane forward. Drag is the air pushing back. If thrust is bigger, the plane speeds up. A smooth shape has less drag.

points.ask: What moves the plane forward?
What slows the plane?
How can we make less drag?

stages.title: Paper aeroplane experiments
stages.hook: You fold two paper planes. One is long and thin. One is short and wide. Which flies further?
explain: A paper plane is a fun way to test flight. You throw it to give it thrust. Then the wings make lift as it moves.
A scientist changes one thing at a time. This is called a fair test. Change only the wing shape and keep the paper, the fold and the throw the same.
Measure how far each plane flies with a tape measure. Try it three times and find the middle result. Fly in a safe space, away from faces and windows.

example.q: You test a plane three times. It flies 4 m, 5 m and 6 m. What is the average?
steps: Add them: 4 + 5 + 6 = 15.
Divide by 3.

analogies.home: Fold a plane from a sheet of paper from the kitchen drawer.
analogies.sport: A javelin thrower tries different throws to go further.
analogies.nature: A bird changes its wing shape to glide further.
analogies.tech: Engineers test small models before they build big planes.

stages.mnemonic: Change one thing, test it three times, write what you find!
terms: Changing only one thing each time.
Find how big or how far.
The middle result of several tries.

misc.wrong: A harder throw always makes a plane fly better.
misc.right: A very hard throw can make a paper plane wobble or dive. A smooth throw and a good fold often work best.

stages.limits: Paper planes are only a small model. Real planes are tested in many other ways too.

trip.prompt: Look at the different folds. Which one looks easiest for a long glide?

questions.q: What do you use to measure how far a plane flies?

o: You cannot tell which change mattered
The plane will not fly at all
Paper is not allowed in tests
Nothing is wrong, it is fine
questions.why: A fair test changes only one thing.

questions.q: A plane flies 3 m, 4 m and 5 m in three tries. What is the average distance in metres?
Put these steps of an experiment in order.

questions.q: Match the change to what it tests.
questions.why: Each change tests one idea.

questions.q: Which is a safe way to fly a paper plane?
o: Throw it away from people's faces

Throw it out of a very high window
Throw it near a busy road

panel.q: Plane A flew 6 m and plane B flew 4 m, each with one try. Can you say A is better?
o: Not yet. You need more tries
No, plane B is always better

panel.why: One try can be luck. More tries show what usually happens.

panel.q: Why does a model help engineers?

panel.q: A plane glides a long way. Which forces are balanced best?

teach.topic: How to do a fair paper plane test
teach.model: Fold two planes and change only one thing, like the wing shape. Throw each plane the same way. Measure how far each one flies. Try three times and find the average.

points.ask: How many things should I change?

stages.title: Spacecraft and rockets
stages.hook: A plane needs air to fly. But space has almost no air. How does a rocket move there?
explain: A rocket burns fuel and pushes hot gas out of the back. The gas goes down, and the rocket goes up. This is like a balloon that zooms when you let the air out.
A rocket carries its own fuel and the air-like stuff it needs to burn it. So a rocket can work in space where there is almost no air.
A spacecraft is a machine that goes to space. It may carry people or tools. Some circle Earth and some travel far away.

example.q: A balloon lets air out of its back. Which way does it go?
steps: The air goes backward.
The balloon is pushed the other way.
So it goes forward.
example.a: Forward, the opposite way to the air

analogies.home: Let go of a blown-up balloon and it zooms around the room.
analogies.sea: A rower pushes water back and the boat goes forward.
analogies.sport: Jump off a skateboard and the board rolls back.
analogies.tech: A fireworks rocket shoots gas down and rises into the sky. Only grown-ups should handle these.

stages.mnemonic: Gas goes down, rocket goes up. Fire out, fly out!
terms: A machine that pushes out gas to move.
A machine that travels in space.

A person who travels in space.

misc.wrong: A rocket pushes against the ground or the air to move.
misc.right: A rocket pushes gas out the back, and the gas pushes the rocket forward. It works with no air at all.

questions.q: What does a rocket push out of its back?
questions.why: A rocket pushes hot gas out the back.

questions.q: A person who travels in space is called an?
questions.why: People who travel in space are astronauts.

questions.q: Can a rocket work where there is almost no air?
questions.why: A rocket carries what it needs and pushes gas out, so it works in space.

questions.why: The air goes one way and the balloon goes the other way.

questions.q: What does a rocket burn?
questions.why: Fuel burns to make hot gas.

questions.q: A plane cannot fly in space. Why?
o: There is almost no air for its wings and engines
Space is far too warm for planes
Space is too noisy for planes
Planes are too big to go up there
questions.why: Wings need air to make lift.

questions.why: First count down, then engines light and the rocket rises.

questions.q: Match each machine to where it goes.
questions.why: Each machine is made for its own place.

questions.q: A rower pushes water back with an oar. What happens to the boat?
questions.why: Pushing back on something makes you move forward. Rockets work the same way.

questions.q: Why does a rocket need lots of fuel?
o: It must push a heavy rocket up fast
Fuel is light, so it helps it float
Fuel is used to make the wings
questions.why: A lot of push is needed to lift a heavy rocket away from Earth.

panel.q: Why does a rocket go up when gas goes down?
o: Pushing one way makes a push the other way
Gas is lighter than air, so it floats up
The ground pushes the rocket up from below
Gravity helps to lift it up high
panel.why: Pushes come in pairs. The rocket pushes gas down and the gas pushes the rocket up.

panel.q: Why does a rocket get lighter as it flies?
o: It burns and throws away fuel
The wings fall off it as it goes
Wind blows it clean as it flies
panel.why: Fuel is used up and thrown out the back, so the rocket loses mass.

panel.q: Which is more like a rocket: a bird or a squid that squirts water?
o: The squid, because it pushes water out to move
The bird, because it has two wings
Neither of them is like a rocket
panel.why: A squid shoots water out and moves the other way, like a rocket.

teach.model: A rocket burns fuel and makes hot gas. It pushes the gas out of the back very fast. The gas pushes the rocket the other way, so it goes up. It works even in space.

points.ask: What comes out of the rocket?
Why does the rocket go up?
Does it need air?

stages.title: Airports and space missions
stages.hook: Many planes land and take off all day at one airport. How do they all stay safe?
explain: An airport has runways for planes to take off and land. A tall control tower stands nearby. People in the tower talk to pilots by radio and say who can go next.
Space missions have a control room too. People on the ground watch the rocket and the spacecraft. They send messages and help the astronauts.
Both need teams. Pilots, engineers, controllers and many helpers work together. Careful plans and checks keep people safe.

example.q: Two planes want to land on one runway. What should the control tower do?
steps: Only one plane can use the runway at a time.
The tower tells one plane to land first.
The other plane waits and flies in a circle.
example.a: Tell one to land and the other to wait

analogies.city: A traffic light tells cars when to go and when to stop. A control tower does this for planes.
analogies.home: A family shares one kitchen and takes turns. Planes share a runway and take turns.
analogies.sea: A harbour master guides ships into port, like a tower guides planes.
analogies.tech: Mission control watches a rocket on big screens.

stages.mnemonic: Tower talks, pilot listens, runway clear, plane glisten!
terms: A long strip where planes take off and land.
A tall building where controllers guide planes.
The ground team that guides a space mission.
The person who flies a plane.

misc.wrong: The pilot flies alone and nobody else helps.
misc.right: Many people help every flight, including controllers, engineers and ground crew.

stages.limits: This is a simple picture. Real airports and missions have many more jobs and rules.

trip.prompt: Find the runway, the tower and a plane on the picture of an airport.

questions.q: Where do planes take off and land?
questions.why: A runway is a long flat strip for planes.

questions.q: Who guides planes from a tall tower?
questions.why: Controllers in the tower guide planes.

questions.q: How do controllers talk to pilots?
questions.why: Radio lets them talk across long distances.

questions.q: What is the team on the ground for a space mission called?
questions.why: Mission control watches and guides the space mission.

questions.q: Why do planes take turns on a runway?
o: Two planes at once would be unsafe
Runways get tired and need rests
Planes like waiting in a long line
Runways are made of thin paper
questions.why: Taking turns keeps everyone safe.

questions.q: A plane has to wait before landing. What does it do?
o: Flies in a circle in the air
Lands on a nearby grass field
Turns off its wings to wait
questions.why: Planes cannot stop in the air, so they fly in a circle until it is their turn.

questions.q: Put these in order for a plane trip.
questions.why: Safe flights start with checks, then take off, flying and landing.

questions.q: Match each worker to the job.
questions.why: Each person has an important job.

questions.q: Why do people check a rocket many times before launch?
o: To keep the crew and the rocket safe
To use up lots of spare time
questions.why: Careful checks find problems before they can hurt anyone.

questions.q: Why is the tower tall?
o: Controllers can see the whole airport
To catch birds in the sky
To make shade for the planes
questions.why: Height gives a good view of runways and planes.

panel.q: Why are airports usually far from the middle of big cities?
o: Planes are loud and need lots of flat space
Planes cannot fly near any people at all
Cities do not have any sky above them
Airports need to be much smaller than cities
panel.why: Runways need a lot of flat, open space, and planes make noise.

panel.q: Why do astronauts need mission control?
o: Teams on the ground can see data and help solve problems
Astronauts cannot think for themselves up there
Mission control flies the rocket just for fun
Rockets cannot be seen from the ground at all
panel.why: Teams share jobs and use many tools to keep the mission safe.

panel.q: Planes take off facing into the wind when they can. Why?
o: More air flows over the wings at a low ground speed
The wind pushes the plane back down to the ground
Wind is noisy, so it hides the engine sound
It does not matter which way it faces
panel.why: Wind toward the plane adds to the airflow over the wings, so lift comes sooner.

teach.model: An airport has runways where planes take off and land. Controllers in a tall tower talk to pilots by radio. They tell each plane when to go or wait, so planes take turns.
